b: AAA-style, player-facing photo mode for Unity: pause the game, fly a free camera, grade the image, apply filter presets and capture supersampled screenshots. The UI is reskinnable and gamepad-ready. Unity 2021.3 LTS or newer · URP, HDRP and the Built-in Render Pipeline.

One-component integration : drop the configured prefab into a scene (or use the Setup Wizard's Add Photo Mode To Scene button) and press your toggle key. Free camera with fly and orbit modes, sprint, roll, FOV zoom, optional collision and a configurable wander radius — plus Animator/Timeline scrubbing to step the frozen scene to the exact frame you want. A full grade stack in natural units : exposure (EV), contrast, saturation, temperature, tint, vignette, film grain, bloom, chromatic aberration, lens distortion, color balance, RGB curves, motion blur, tilt-shift, sharpen, an HSL qualifier and bokeh depth of field with a perceptual f-stop slider (per-pipeline availability in the pipeline notes ). Runtime relighting : up to six photo lights (key, fill, rim and more) you orbit around your subject, with scene-light dimming — all torn down and restored exactly on exit. Physical camera : focal length in millimeters on real sensor presets and a coupled f-stop / shutter / ISO exposure triangle with a live EV readout, on all three pipelines. Six filter presets (Clean, Noir, Vivid, Warm, Cool, Vintage) and 24 LUT filters with an intensity slider, plus .cube import and export of your current look, your own preset assets and an automatic Custom state. Supersampled and tiled capture : 1×/2×/4× supersampling with async GPU readback, and tiled 8K/16K/32K capture past the GPU texture limit; PNG output, optional transparent background, thumbnail toast and a capture event for your own pipelines. Render layer (AOV) export : depth, normals, albedo, object-ID mattes and alpha beside every capture — on URP and Built-in as well as HDRP. In-game gallery : favorites, multi-select, two-step delete, per-photo metadata and Go To Shot , which re-frames the camera to where a saved photo was taken. Capture Studio : a dockable editor window that composes and renders shot lists in Edit Mode, with a headless command-line entry point for CI. All three render pipelines : URP, HDRP and Built-in (Post Processing Stack v2 or a minimal fallback). The backend is detected automatically, and controls hide themselves when the active pipeline can't apply an effect. WebGL, Android touch and 2D games : WebGL captures persist in the gallery across page reloads and download on demand, the UI works with touch gestures, and orthographic games get a pan/zoom camera that behaves like one. Both input systems : the new Input System, the legacy Input Manager, or Both . Keyboard + mouse and gamepad, with full UI navigation. Zero per-frame GC allocations while open and idle or dragging sliders, and no per-frame work while closed. IL2CPP + high stripping verified.
Quick Start : the 2-minute wizard path and the manual path. Core Concepts : how the controller, backends and UI fit together. Troubleshooting : if something looks wrong.

In the editor: Tools → Photo Mode Pro → Report a Bug (pre-filled email), or write to support.dan.max@gmail.com . Tools → Photo Mode Pro → Run Self-Test writes a PhotoModeSelfTest.json you can attach to any report.
Two ways in: the wizard path (about 2 minutes) or the manual path (about 10).

Unity 2021.3 LTS or newer (verified on 2021.3, 2022.3 and 6000.3). Any render pipeline: URP (12+), HDRP (12+) or Built-in . On Built-in, install com.unity.postprocessing (Post Processing Stack v2) for the full adjustment set; without it a minimal fallback backend is used. The right backend is detected automatically at runtime (override via PhotoModeSettings.BackendOverride ). Optional: the Input System package (recommended). The legacy Input Manager also works; see Integrations for its gamepad limitations.

Import Photo Mode Pro. A welcome window appears on first import (once per machine), or open Tools → Photo Mode Pro → Setup Wizard any time. The wizard checks your render pipeline, effects backend, input handling, optional packages, TextMesh Pro essentials and the demo materials, each with a green / yellow / red light, a one-line explanation and a Fix button where a fix can be automated (importing TMP essentials, rebuilding the demo for your pipeline). Open your scene and press Add Photo Mode To Scene . The configured prefab (settings, six presets, UI) lands in the scene, selected. Press Play, then press F (or the gamepad View/Share button). You're in. No EventSystem? No problem. If your scene has no EventSystem when photo mode opens, one is created for the duration (matching your active input handling) and removed on exit. The scene is left exactly as found.

Drag Assets/PhotoModePro/Demo/Generated/PhotoModePro.prefab into your scene (menu equivalent: Tools → Photo Mode Pro → Add Photo Mode To Scene ). The prefab already references the default PhotoModeSettings , the UI prefab and the six built-in presets. Done. Press your toggle key in Play mode. Recommended wiring on the PhotoModeController component: Game Ui Canvases : add your HUD canvases so photo mode can hide them. Player Objects : add your player root(s) for the Hide Player toggle. To change keys, pause behavior, camera limits or the save folder, duplicate PhotoModeSettings.asset (or create one via Assets → Create → Photo Mode Pro → Settings ) and assign it on the controller.

Open Assets/PhotoModePro/Demo/PhotoModeDemo.unity : a forest clearing at golden hour with a campfire, wandering animals and a playable adventurer (all bundled third-party assets are CC0; see Demo/ThirdParty/ATTRIBUTIONS.md ). Press Play. Move with WASD (or left stick), orbit with the mouse (or right stick), Shift to run, Space to jump. Press F to open photo mode. Fire, animals and audio freeze instantly. Try the Warm preset against the sunset, or pull focus with depth of field. Demo on HDRP or Built-in The demo generates its materials for your active pipeline. If you open the demo scene under a different pipeline than it was last built for, a dialog offers Rebuild demo for current pipeline (also available from the Setup Wizard). The demo is never pink. The Demo folder is safe to delete. Everything demo-related lives under Assets/PhotoModePro/Demo/ and nothing outside it references that folder. The generated controller/UI prefabs, settings, theme and presets live under Demo/Generated/ ; if you delete the demo, create your own settings asset and add the PhotoModeController component directly (the Add Photo Mode To Scene menu does this for you and explains what to assign).

Photo Mode Pro is built around one component, one settings asset and a handful of small, replaceable pieces. This page explains how they fit together so the how-to guides make sense at a glance.

PhotoModeController (menu: Photo Mode Pro/Photo Mode Controller ) is the single entry point. Add it to any GameObject (or drop in the generated prefab), assign a PhotoModeSettings asset, and you are done. The component is marked [DisallowMultipleComponent] , and if a second controller appears in the scene it disables itself with a warning: there is always at most one active controller. Scripts reach it through the null-safe static accessor: using PhotoModePro ; PhotoModeController photoMode = PhotoModeController . Instance ; // null when none is enabled Instance is set in OnEnable and cleared in OnDisable , so it is safe across scene loads. See Events & API for the full scripting surface.

EnterPhotoMode() (or the configured toggle binding, F / View by default) does, in order: Records the current Time.timeScale , AudioListener.pause , cursor visibility, cursor lock state and the main camera's enabled flag. Pauses the game per PhotoModeSettings.PauseMode ( TimeScaleZero by default, or Unscaled to keep the game running) and audio per AudioPauseMode . Clones the camera tagged MainCamera into a free photo camera (carrying over URP/HDRP camera data) and disables the original. Creates the effects backend for the active render pipeline and applies the current adjustments. Hides your registered game UI canvases and spawns the photo mode UI prefab. ExitPhotoMode() restores exactly what it found: the recorded timeScale , audio pause state, cursor state and main-camera enabled flag, destroys the photo camera and UI, and re-shows anything the visibility toggles hid. If the scene had no EventSystem when the UI opened, photo mode creates a matching one and removes it again on exit. The scene is left exactly as found. Cinemachine-driven cameras hand off and resume cleanly too; see Integrations . Safety nets Replacing or unloading a scene while photo mode is open auto-closes it cleanly (state restored first, an in-flight capture abandoned). Additive loads (streamed chunks) are harmless and do not close the session. If the controller itself is destroyed while open, an OnDestroy fallback still restores time scale, audio, cursor and everything photo mode spawned. EnterPhotoMode() no-ops when already active or when no main camera exists; ExitPhotoMode() no-ops while inactive or while a capture is in flight.

PhotoModeController.Adjustments is a plain PhotoModeAdjustments object holding every image tweak in natural units . No pipeline types anywhere: Field Unit / range Neutral ExposureEv EV, −3 .. +3 0 Contrast , Saturation , Temperature −100 .. +100 0 Vignette , FilmGrain 0 .. 1 0 DepthOfFieldEnabled bool off FocusDistance meters 10 Aperture f-number (applied clamped to f/0.7–f/16) f/5.6 Values are sticky for the play session : close and reopen photo mode and your look is still there. If you write fields from script, call controller.NotifyAdjustmentsEdited() afterwards; details in Image adjustments .

Adjustments are pushed through IPhotoModeEffectsBackend (namespace PhotoModePro.Effects ), a small render-pipeline abstraction. Four implementations ship in the box: URP volume, HDRP volume (physical-camera depth of field), Post Processing Stack v2, and a minimal Built-in fallback shader. Selection is automatic from the active render pipeline; force one via PhotoModeSettings.BackendOverride if you must. Each backend reports EffectCapabilities flags ( Exposure , Contrast , Saturation , Temperature , Vignette , Grain , DepthOfField , TransparentCapture , Bloom , ChromaticAberration , LensDistortion , TiltShift , Sharpen , MotionBlur , Tint , ColorBalance , Curves , HslQualifier ). The UI hides any control whose capability is missing , so players never touch a dead slider, and gamepad navigation never lands on one. Scripts read the same flags via PhotoModeController.ActiveCapabilities . That works even while photo mode is closed, where it returns a prediction for the backend that would be selected right now. Per-pipeline differences are tabulated in Pipelines .

PhotoModeSettings ( Assets > Create > Photo Mode Pro > Settings ) holds every tunable: key/gamepad bindings, pause and audio behavior, free-camera limits (speed, sphere clamp, collision, FOV range, roll speed), the effects backend override, capture defaults and the save path, and visibility options. Duplicate it per configuration and assign it on the controller, or swap it from script via the Settings property while photo mode is inactive.

A PhotoModePreset asset is just a named bundle of adjustment values. Six ship built in (Clean, Noir, Vivid, Warm, Cool, Vintage); the controller's Presets list decides what the Presets tab offers. ApplyPreset(preset) copies the values in; ApplyPreset(null) resets to the neutral "Clean" state. See Presets .

The photo mode UI is an ordinary UGUI prefab ( PhotoModeUIController ) that the controller instantiates on enter and destroys on exit. It has six categories (Camera, Light, Effects, Presets, Capture, Gallery) cycled with Q/E or LB/RB , full keyboard/gamepad navigation, and a single row of hotkey hint chips along the bottom edge of the screen. Every color, sprite, font, motion parameter and UI sound comes from one PhotoModeUITheme asset; swap it to reskin everything. See Theming .

CapturePhoto() (or P / the SNAP button) renders the photo camera into a RenderTexture at 1×, 2× or 4× the screen resolution ( Supersample ), with temporal anti-aliasing and dynamic resolution disabled for the shot so the output is artifact-free and exactly the requested size. The result is read back with AsyncGPUReadback where the platform supports it, encoded to PNG with a timestamped, collision-safe file name, and saved to {persistentDataPath}/Photos (or PhotoModeSettings.CustomSavePath ). A thumbnail toast confirms the shot, and OnPhotoCaptured(path, thumbnail) fires for your own code. Heavy supersampled captures show a "PROCESSING…" badge that never appears in the photo. Full details in Capturing photos ; timing numbers live in Performance .

When photo mode opens, the main camera is cloned into a free photo camera driven by a FreeCameraController . It runs on unscaled time (so it works while the game is frozen) and allocates nothing per frame.

Mode Behavior Fly (default) Free flight: WASD / left stick moves, Space / Left Ctrl (triggers) elevate, mouse / right stick looks. Orbit The camera circles the activation point (where photo mode was opened) at an adjustable distance. Look input orbits; forward/back input changes the orbit distance. Switch in the UI's Camera tab (Fly / Orbit buttons) or from script. Switching preserves the current framing. The starting mode comes from PhotoModeSettings.DefaultCameraMode .

Action Keyboard / Mouse Gamepad Move / fly WASD, Space up, Left Ctrl down Left stick, triggers up/down Look Hold right mouse button Right stick Sprint Left Shift Left stick click Roll Z / C Roll slider (Camera tab) Zoom (FOV) Mouse wheel FOV slider (Camera tab) Notes: Sprint multiplies both move speed and roll speed by PhotoModeSettings.SprintMultiplier . Wheel zoom only acts when the pointer is not over the UI (over the side panel the wheel scrolls the panel). It moves the FOV slider live, two-way. The FOV slider range follows PhotoModeSettings.MinFov / MaxFov (10–120° by default).

The Camera tab carries a row of framing aids: Aid What it shows Guides Cycles composition guide overlays: off, thirds, golden ratio, diagonal. Horizon A center line that counter-rotates with the camera's roll and changes color when the horizon is level (within half a degree). Histogram A live luminance histogram of the current frame. Focus peaking Highlights in-focus edges, for nailing focus with depth of field. Clipping zebras Stripes over blown-out (clipped) areas of the frame. All of these are preview-only overlays — they never appear in captured photos . From script, FocusPeaking , ClippingZebras and HistogramVisible on PhotoModeController toggle the same aids; see Events & API .

Both are configured on the settings asset : Setting Meaning MaxDistance Max distance from the activation point, in meters (sphere clamp). Default 15; 0 = unlimited. EnableCollision Sphere-cast the camera against geometry so it cannot clip through walls. Off by default. CollisionRadius Radius of that sphere cast (default 0.2 m). CollisionMask Layers the camera collides with. Note The sphere clamp is your spoiler/exploit guard. It keeps players from flying the camera across the level. The activation point is exposed as FreeCameraController.Pivot .

PhotoModeController.PhotoCamera returns the FreeCameraController while photo mode is active, and null otherwise: using PhotoModePro ; using UnityEngine ; FreeCameraController cam = PhotoModeController . Instance . PhotoCamera ; if ( cam != null ) { cam . Mode = PhotoModeCameraMode . Orbit ; // or call cam.SetMode(...) cam . Fov = 35f ; // clamped to settings.MinFov..MaxFov cam . Roll = 10f ; // degrees, wrapped to -180..180 cam . MoveSpeed = 12f ; // meters/second, min 0.1 Debug . Log ( $"Orbit pivot: {cam.Pivot}" ); } The component lives on the spawned photo camera GameObject, so cam.transform / cam.GetComponent<Camera>() give you the actual camera if you need to read its pose or projection. Physical cameras (HDRP) While the camera uses physical properties, the controller drives zoom via focalLength instead of fieldOfView . Writing fieldOfView would silently switch the camera back to non-physical mode and break HDRP's depth of field. Use the Fov property and let the controller pick the right path. Position and rotation are smoothed exponentially ( PhotoModeSettings.Smoothing , 0 disables smoothing), so script writes to Fov / Roll ease in rather than snapping. Related: Image adjustments · Capturing photos · Events & API

Switch the Camera tab's Physical Camera toggle on and the photo camera stops being a FOV slider and becomes a camera: focal length in millimeters on a real sensor, and an exposure triangle — f-stop, shutter speed, ISO — coupled the way a photographer expects. Unity's own physical camera properties drive exposure and depth of field under HDRP only ; on URP and Built-in they are inert with respect to the post stack. Photo Mode Pro's model works on all three.

Focal Length (12–200 mm) and the sensor preset (Full Frame, APS-C, Micro 4/3, Super 35, 16 mm) drive the field of view through real lens geometry — 24 mm feels wide, 85 mm compresses a portrait, and the same lens gets tighter on a crop sensor, exactly as it should. While the model is on, the FOV slider hides (the lens owns it); switch the toggle off to return to direct FOV control.

F-Stop , Shutter and ISO snap to the standard photographic stop sequences (f/0.7–f/16, 1/1000 s–1 s, ISO 100–6400) with a live EV readout. With Lock Exposure on (the default), the triangle is coupled: open the aperture two stops and the shutter compensates two stops the other way — constant exposure, different look. Each leg drives its photographic consequence: Leg Drives F-stop Depth-of-field strength — the same public Adjustments.Aperture as always, so nothing breaks Shutter Motion-blur weight (where the pipeline offers the effect) ISO Film-grain intensity — base ISO is clean, ISO 6400 is gritty EV delta Exposure compensation when you unlock the triangle On pipelines that cannot express a coupling (the Built-in fallback has no depth of field, for example) the control stays visible and functional for the legs it can drive — reported through capabilities, never silently swallowed. Blades shapes the bokeh via the aperture blade count where the pipeline supports it (HDRP); the row hides elsewhere. On HDRP the photo camera itself runs in physical mode (focal length, sensor, aperture, shutter, ISO and blade count on the camera), so HDRP's own physical depth of field and exposure respond too.

The physical model only ever touches the photo camera — the clone that exists while photo mode is open. Your game's camera keeps its own properties, untouched, before, during and after; the model's state persists across photo sessions so your lens setup is still there next time.

var controller = PhotoModeController . Instance ; var physical = controller . PhysicalCamera ; physical . Enabled = true ; physical . CaptureBaseEv (); // lock the current exposure physical . FocalLengthMm = 85f ; // plain field, no coupling physical . SetAperture ( 1.4f ); // shutter compensates automatically controller . NotifyPhysicalCameraEdited (); Drive the exposure legs through SetAperture / SetShutter / SetIso : writing the Aperture , ShutterSeconds or Iso fields directly skips both the clamping and the exposure coupling (the values are only clamped later, as a backstop, when the model is applied). FocalLengthMm has no coupling, so the field write above is fine. PhotoModeExposureTriangle exposes the pure math (EV, compensation, stop snapping, lens geometry) if you want the relationships without the model.

The Light tab is a full lighting rig that exists only inside photo mode: add up to six photo lights, orbit them around your subject, tune color and intensity, dim the scene's own lights — and everything is torn down and restored exactly when you leave. No other Unity asset offers runtime light placement as a photo-mode capability; the lighting tools on the store are editor-side preset managers. Rig lights live under a root object the system creates ( PhotoModePro Light Rig ), never inside your scene hierarchy, and are destroyed on exit. Scene lights you touch through the rig are snapshotted before the first change and restored field-for-field on exit, under the same contract as time scale, audio and cursor state.

The five add buttons create a light pre-configured for a photographic role: Kind Type Starts as Key Spot Bright warm-neutral, ahead-left of the subject, 35° above the horizon Fill Point Soft cool light opposite the key, no shadows Rim Spot Hard white light behind the subject for edge separation Practical Point Small warm lantern-style glow near the subject Sun Directional Scene-wide golden light Rig presets replace the current rig with a complete setup: Three-Point, Rembrandt, Rim Only, Golden Hour, Moonlight and Practical Warm. Apply one, then edit any light it created.

Placement is free: put the light anywhere. The primary tool is the mouse — grab the light's on-screen marker and drag it, and it follows the cursor exactly, moving in the camera-parallel plane through the light (turn or move the camera and drag again to move in depth). Clicking a marker selects that light. The panel shows the position as live, unbounded X / Y / Z world coordinates with step buttons for fine, gamepad-friendly adjustment, plus: Distance — meters from the focus point (the spot photo mode opened at); sliding it moves the light radially toward or away from your subject. Lights always aim at the focus point, so wherever you put one, it lights your subject. Markers are tinted with their light's color, hide with the rest of the UI ( H ), and can never appear in a capture. Follow Camera anchors the orbit to the camera view instead of the world: the whole setup travels with the shot as you re-frame, so a rim stays a rim.

Type cycles Point → Spot → Area → Sun where the active pipeline supports them (realtime area lights exist on HDRP only; the option is hidden elsewhere). Intensity is entered in Unity intensity units everywhere. On HDRP — which lights in physical units — the readout converts to real photometric values: lumens for point, spot and area lights, lux for directional, so the same slider position reads comparably on every pipeline. Hue / Color Sat set the light color (saturation 0 is white). Range , Spot Angle and Shadows behave exactly like their Unity counterparts; controls that do not apply to the current type hide themselves.

The Scene Lights slider is a master dimmer for the scene's own lighting: every light that was already in the scene and the ambient environment (ambient intensity and colors, reflection intensity). Pull it down to darken the game's lighting, then build the shot with rig lights alone. This slider is the relight mechanism, not a garnish. Physically, a rig light follows the inverse-square law — at typical distances it adds only a few units of illumination, invisible against daylight. Darkening the frame with negative exposure does not help: exposure attenuates the rig's own contribution equally. Dim the scene instead and the rig owns the light; even modest intensities read like studio strobes against a dimmed base. The dimmer also darkens the sky. Skybox scenes get a session copy of the skybox material with its exposure (or tint) scaled down; skybox-less scenes have their solid-color camera backgrounds scaled instead. One exception: a custom skybox shader that exposes no _Exposure , _Tint , _TintColor or _Color property cannot be dimmed and keeps its authored brightness. The slider scales realtime lighting only. Baked lights — and the baked half of Mixed lights — live in the lightmaps, which the dimmer cannot touch, so their contribution stays at full brightness (a warning is logged when the scene contains such lights). Everything the dimmer touches is snapshotted on first use and restored exactly on exit. The dim level is saved into Capture Studio bookmarks and user looks, so a relit shot reproduces with its intended base. On HDRP the dimmer scales scene lights only: HDRP's ambient comes from its sky and exposure system, not RenderSettings , so the ambient term is left to your volume setup there (a physically exposed HDRP scene usually responds well to dimming the sun alone).

Everything the tab does is public API: var controller = PhotoModeController . Instance ; controller . EnterPhotoMode (); // Add and edit a rig light. var rig = controller . LightRig ; var key = rig . AddLight ( PhotoModeLightKind . Key ); key . Color = Color . cyan ; key . Intensity = 3f ; rig . NotifyLightEdited ( key ); // Modify a scene light under the exact-restore contract. var snapshot = rig . TrackSceneLight ( mySceneLight ); mySceneLight . intensity = 0.1f ; controller . ExitPhotoMode (); // rig destroyed, mySceneLight restored exactly PhotoModeController.ActiveLightingCapabilities reports what the active pipeline supports (point/spot/directional/area lights, shadows, physical units) — the same honest capability gating the effects system uses, so the Light tab hides itself entirely on pipelines with no lighting backend. Rig presets are plain ScriptableObjects ( PhotoModeLightPreset ): create your own via Assets → Create → Photo Mode Pro → Light Preset and assign them to the controller's Light Presets list.

The Effects tab exposes the full adjustment set. Every value lives in PhotoModeController.Adjustments (a PhotoModeAdjustments object) in natural, pipeline-agnostic units, and is sticky for the play session.

Control Field Unit / range Notes Exposure ExposureEv EV, −3 .. +3 Relative exposure compensation; identical semantics on every pipeline (on HDRP it maps to post-exposure, so it never fights auto-exposure). Contrast Contrast −100 .. +100 0 is neutral. Saturation Saturation −100 .. +100 −100 is grayscale. Temperature Temperature −100 (cool) .. +100 (warm) 0 is neutral. Vignette Vignette 0 .. 1 Edge softness differs slightly per pipeline. Grain FilmGrain 0 .. 1 Response normalized across pipelines; subtle character differences remain. Depth of Field DepthOfFieldEnabled toggle The two rows below hide while this is off. Focus Dist FocusDistance meters, 0.1 .. 100 (slider) Logarithmic slider: half the travel covers the visibly focus-pulling 0.1–3 m. The readout stays in meters. Aperture Aperture f-number, f/0.7 .. f/16 (slider) See below.

The aperture slider spans f/0.7 – f/16 with a perceptual log-stop mapping: each step of slider travel multiplies the f-number by a constant ratio, so a nudge near f/1 changes the bokeh about as much as a nudge near f/11, the way photographers think in stops. Lower f-numbers mean a shallower focus plane and bigger bokeh; f/0.7 is the widest aperture HDRP's physical camera accepts, and beyond ~f/16 the blur is sub-pixel at game scales. Clamping PhotoModeAdjustments.Aperture still accepts any positive value from script, and old presets keep loading unchanged, but the effect backends clamp into [PhotoModeAdjustments.APERTURE_MIN, APERTURE_MAX] (0.7–16) when applying. A preset saved at f/22 simply renders as f/16.

Not every backend supports every effect. The Built-in fallback (no Post Processing Stack v2) lacks temperature, grain and depth of field, and HDRP cannot do transparent captures. Unsupported controls hide automatically , and scripts can check the same flags: using PhotoModePro ; using PhotoModePro.Effects ; bool hasDof = ( PhotoModeController . Instance . ActiveCapabilities & EffectCapabilities . DepthOfField ) != 0 ; The full capability matrix and the visual differences between pipelines are on the Pipelines page.

Write the fields directly, then tell the controller you did. That marks the effects dirty (re-applied next frame) and flips the preset label to "Custom": using PhotoModePro ; var controller = PhotoModeController . Instance ; controller . Adjustments . ExposureEv = 0.5f ; controller . Adjustments . Saturation = - 100f ; // grayscale controller . Adjustments . Vignette = 0.35f ; controller . Adjustments . DepthOfFieldEnabled = true ; controller . Adjustments . FocusDistance = 2.5f ; // meters controller . Adjustments . Aperture = 1.4f ; // f-stops controller . NotifyAdjustmentsEdited (); Warning Without NotifyAdjustmentsEdited() your changes sit in the model but never reach the screen until something else (a slider, a preset) triggers a re-apply. The UI sliders call it for you; direct field writes must. To replace the whole set at once, use a preset instead: ApplyPreset(...) copies values, re-applies and raises OnAdjustmentsReplaced so the UI re-seeds its sliders. See Presets . Values for capabilities the active backend lacks are simply ignored (never clamped or destroyed), so a look authored on URP survives a session on the Built-in fallback intact. Related: Core Concepts · Presets · Events & API

Version 1.1 grows the adjustment set from 7 to 18. Beside the originals: Control Range Notes Bloom 0..1 Comparable response on URP, HDRP and PPv2. Chromatic Ab 0..1 Edge fringing. Distortion −100..+100 Pincushion to barrel. Tilt-Shift 0..1 Miniature band blur — identical on every pipeline (rendered by the package, not the pipeline). Sharpen 0..1 Unsharp mask, pipeline-independent. Motion Blur 0..1 URP and HDRP (the effect needs motion vectors). Tint Hue / Amount 0..360 / 0..1 Multiplicative color filter. Shadows / Midtones / Highlights −100..+100 each Warm/cool balance per tonal band. RGB curves — a gamepad-native curve editor: pick the channel (Master, Red, Green, Blue) and shape it with three control points at the 25/50/75% inputs. The same curves bake into the .cube export. HSL qualifier — a true secondary: select a hue range (center + width), then shift its hue, saturation and lightness without touching the rest of the frame. Turn the one red jacket teal; leave the world alone. Controls a pipeline cannot express hide themselves with the reason documented in the per-pipeline notes — nothing silently no-ops.

A preset is a PhotoModePreset asset: a display name plus one full set of adjustment values . There are no LUT textures or shaders involved, just plain data, so presets stay tiny and diff cleanly in version control.

Preset Look Clean Neutral: every value at its default. First in the list and the active default. Noir High-contrast desaturated black & white. Vivid Punchy contrast and saturation. Warm Golden-hour temperature shift. Cool Blue-shifted, moody. Vintage Faded grain-and-vignette film look. Clean is the default state : PhotoModeController.CurrentPresetLabel reads "Clean" when photo mode opens and after any reset.

Assets > Create > Photo Mode Pro > Preset . Set DisplayName , the label shown on the Presets tab button. Fill in the Adjustments block (same fields and units as the Effects tab : EV, −100..+100, 0..1, meters, f-stops). Author presets live Enter Play mode, dial in a look with the sliders, then copy the values into your preset asset. The component Inspector and the asset use identical fields, so it is a one-to-one transfer. Aperture range Aperture values outside f/0.7–f/16 are accepted by the asset but clamped by the effect backends when applied; see the aperture slider .

The controller's Presets list (Inspector field, or the Presets property from script) decides which presets the Presets tab shows, in order: using PhotoModePro ; var controller = PhotoModeController . Instance ; controller . Presets . Add ( myPreset ); // List<PhotoModePreset> The generated prefab ships with the built-in six already assigned; change the list however you like.

using PhotoModePro ; var controller = PhotoModeController . Instance ; controller . ApplyPreset ( myPreset ); // copies values in, re-applies effects controller . ApplyPreset ( null ); // programmatic reset -> neutral "Clean" state ApplyPreset copies the preset's values into controller.Adjustments , pushes them to the effects backend and raises OnAdjustmentsReplaced (so the UI sliders re-seed). ApplyPreset(null) resets every value to neutral, identical to the Clean preset.

t: The label: Clean, a preset name, or "Custom"
b: CurrentPresetLabel tracks where the current look came from: State Label Neutral (open, or after ApplyPreset(null) ) "Clean" A preset was applied the preset's DisplayName Any slider moved (or NotifyAdjustmentsEdited() called) after that "Custom" The label is sticky for the play session, like the adjustment values themselves. The UI shows it so players always know whether they are on a stock look or have drifted from it. Related: Image adjustments · Core Concepts · Events & API

The Presets tab carries 24 LUT filters — from Teal & Orange and Bleach Bypass to Cyber Neon and Frostbite — with an intensity slider to dial each one in. They are not hand-painted textures: every filter is an adjustment recipe baked through the package's own grade pipeline into a 33³ LUT at build time, and they apply through the pipeline-independent presenter, so a filter looks the same on URP, HDRP and Built-in.

In the editor — create Assets → Create → Photo Mode Pro → LUT Filter and assign any LUT strip texture (width = size², height = size). It appears in the filter list automatically. At runtime — drop .cube files or strip PNGs into the LUTs folder next to your photos and press IMPORT LUTS : industry-standard cube files from DaVinci Resolve, Premiere or anywhere else load directly.

EXPORT .CUBE bakes the current adjustment chain — exposure, contrast, curves, tint, balance, everything color — into a 33³ LUT and writes an industry-standard .cube file to the LUTs folder. Import is table stakes; the export is the engineering half: grade a shot in photo mode, then carry that exact look into DaVinci, Premiere, OBS or another Unity project. A round-trip test guards the fidelity: bake → write → re-parse → applying the parsed LUT reproduces the baked look exactly at every grid point.

Players can save their own looks — the full adjustment set plus the relight rig — name them, reload them and delete them from the Presets tab. Looks are plain JSON files in a Looks folder beside the photos; the files are the export format. Copy a .look.json to another machine or project and it loads as-is; the LUT filter travels by name.

Press P (keyboard), X / Square (gamepad) or the SNAP button, or call PhotoModeController.CapturePhoto() from script. The UI hides itself for the shot, the frame is rendered offscreen, encoded to PNG and saved to disk, and a thumbnail toast confirms it.

The Capture tab offers 1× / 2× / 4× output resolution ( PhotoModeController.Supersample , default from PhotoModeSettings.DefaultSupersample ). A 4× capture of a 1080p view renders at 7680×4320. Temporal anti-aliasing and dynamic resolution are disabled for the duration of every capture, so the output is artifact-free and exactly the requested size. Heavy captures show a badge Supersampled captures block the main thread for the render + encode. A static PROCESSING… badge appears automatically for 2×/4× shots. It lives on the overlay canvas and can never end up in the photo. Expect multiple seconds at 4× from 1080p; measured timings are on the Performance page. The readback uses AsyncGPUReadback where the platform supports it, with a synchronous fallback elsewhere.

Setting Result PhotoModeSettings.CustomSavePath empty (default) {Application.persistentDataPath}/Photos CustomSavePath set that directory, used verbatim PhotoModeController.SaveDirectory returns the resolved directory at runtime. The save-path row on the Capture tab is clickable and opens the folder; clicking the capture toast reveals the new file (Windows Explorer reveal; folder open on other platforms). File naming: {ProductName}_{yyyy-MM-dd_HH-mm-ss}.png , with the product name sanitized for the file system. Collisions get a counter suffix: Game_2026-06-11_12-00-00_001.png .

Toggle Transparent BG on the Capture tab (or set PhotoModeController.TransparentCapture ) to capture with a clean alpha channel, useful for compositing screenshots over other art. Warning Transparent frames render without post-processing (post effects destroy alpha), so your image adjustments do not appear in transparent shots. Not available on HDRP : the toggle is hidden there and a transparent request is ignored at the backend boundary. URP and both Built-in backends support it. Details on Pipelines .

Toggle Hotkey What it does Hide UI H / Y (Triangle) Hides the photo mode chrome for a clean preview. Capture feedback (flash, toast) stays visible. Hide Game UI Capture tab Hides the canvases registered on the controller ( GameUiCanvases list + GameUiTag ). On by default when AutoHideGameUi is set. Hide Player Capture tab Disables the renderers of the registered player objects ( PlayerObjects list + PlayerTag ). Animator/physics state is untouched, so unhiding never pops. Hide Layers Capture tab Removes PhotoModeSettings.HiddenLayers from the photo camera's culling mask. All of these are restored exactly on exit. Scripts can drive them through PhotoModeController.Visibility ( SetGameUiHidden / SetPlayerHidden / SetLayersHidden ).

using PhotoModePro ; using UnityEngine ; void Start () { // Instance is assigned in the controller's OnEnable, so subscribe from // Start() (or null-check first) rather than Awake/OnEnable. PhotoModeController . Instance . OnPhotoCaptured += HandlePhoto ; } void HandlePhoto ( string path , Texture2D thumbnail ) { Debug . Log ( $"Photo saved to {path}" ); // The thumbnail belongs to photo mode and is destroyed on the next // capture (or on exit); copy it before keeping a reference. To use the // full image, load the saved file at `path` instead. } The thumbnail is owned by photo mode: it is destroyed on the next capture or when photo mode exits, so copy it (for example with Graphics.CopyTexture into a texture you own) if you want to keep it past the event. It can also be null for a successfully saved photo when rendering the small preview failed, so null-check before using it. The same event exists as a UnityEvent ( On Photo Captured ) on the controller for Inspector wiring. IsCapturing is true while a capture is in flight. ExitPhotoMode() no-ops during that window, and the toggle key is ignored. Related: Core Concepts · Events & API · Troubleshooting

Tools → Photo Mode Pro → Capture Studio opens a dockable editor window that drives the same camera, grade stack and relight rig as the runtime photo mode — in Edit Mode, without pressing Play. Compose shots, bookmark them, and render whole batches at real publishing resolutions. No other photo-mode asset has an editor side at all; no capture asset in the category offers CI-driven shot lists. In Play Mode with photo mode open, the studio binds to the live session: the window and the in-game UI edit the same shot. HDRP: Play Mode only HDRP's color grading does not apply reliably to Edit Mode camera renders (verified with the StandardRequest pipeline-render API), so on HDRP the studio (and the headless entry point) runs in Play Mode — the window says so instead of rendering wrong colors. For an exact grade preview on HDRP, open photo mode so the studio binds to the live session.

Preview — a live render of the studio camera, letterboxed to the selected output preset's aspect, with an optional 5% crop-safe-area overlay. Camera — grab the Scene View camera with one click, or set position, rotation and FOV numerically. Grade — the core adjustment set (exposure, contrast, saturation, temperature, vignette, grain, depth of field), applied through the same pipeline backends as the runtime. Light Rig — add key/fill/rim/practical/sun lights, orbit them around the focus point, tune color and intensity. Studio rig objects are session-flagged: they never dirty or save into your scene. Shot List — bookmarks with apply/reorder/delete, saved into a PhotoModeShotList asset. Render — render the current view to any output preset, or Render All to write the entire matrix.

A bookmark stores everything a shot needs: camera pose and lens, the complete adjustment set, the focus point and the full light rig. Save View as Bookmark captures the current state; Apply restores it exactly — in Edit Mode or Play Mode.

PhotoModeOutputPreset assets define exact pixel targets: dimensions, PNG or 16/32-bit EXR, supersampling, transparent background, and a watermark slot (texture, corner, offset, opacity, scale) composited at output resolution , never at preview resolution. The built-in set covers real targets: Preset Size Asset Store Key Image 1950×1300 Asset Store Card / Icon 420×280 / 160×160 Steam Capsules (Main / Small / Header / Library) 616×353 / 231×87 / 460×215 / 600×900 App Store Screenshot 6.5" 1284×2778 Play Store Screenshot / Feature Graphic 1080×1920 / 1024×500 Press Kit 4K 3840×2160 Wallpapers 1920×1080, 2560×1440 Create your own via Assets → Create → Photo Mode Pro → Output Preset .

A PhotoModeShotList asset is a matrix: bookmarks × grade presets × output presets . Leave the grade-preset list empty and each bookmark renders with its own saved look; add presets (Noir, Warm, …) and every bookmark renders once per look. File names are deterministic and collision-safe: {list}_{bookmark}_{preset}_{output}.{png|exr} .

The same matrix renders from the command line — regenerate your entire store asset pack on every build: Unity -batchmode -quit -projectPath . ^ -executeMethod PhotoModePro.Editor.CaptureStudio.PhotoModeHeadlessCapture.RenderShotList ^ -photomode-shotlist Assets/Marketing/StoreSet.asset ^ -photomode-capture-out Renders ^ -photomode-capture-result TestResults/shotlist_result.json ^ -photomode-scene Assets/Scenes/Showcase.unity The JSON result mirrors the package self-test's shape: environment fields ( ProductVersion reports the installed package version) plus one record per shot with pass/fail, path, dimensions, format and wall time — ready for a CI gate: { "Pass" : true , "ProductVersion" : "x.y.z" , "Pipeline" : "Urp" , "Shots" : [ { "Name" : "StoreSet_Hero_KeyImage.png" , "Status" : "Ok" , "Width" : 1950 , "Height" : 1300 , "Format" : "Png" , "WallTimeMs" : 412 } ] } -photomode-scene is optional — omit it to render whatever scene the project opens with.

Beside every capture, Photo Mode Pro can export the render layers a compositor works with — depth, normals, albedo, object-ID mattes and alpha — as EXR and PNG files. Unity itself ships arbitrary output variables (AOVs) HDRP-only ; Photo Mode Pro brings the layer set to URP and the Built-in pipeline through its own capture path, with per-pipeline capability gating and zero changes to your renderer assets.

Layer File Format Contents Beauty photo.png PNG The normal graded capture. Depth photo_depth.exr 32-bit float EXR Linear 0–1 view depth (1 = far plane). Normals photo_normal.exr 16-bit half EXR World-space normals packed to 0–1, including material normal maps. Albedo photo_albedo.png PNG Unlit base color exactly as authored. Object IDs photo_id.png + photo_id_map.json PNG A distinct flat color per object, with a name→color sidecar. Alpha photo_alpha.png PNG The clean-alpha coverage of the shot as grayscale. Matte photo_matte.png PNG White-on-black selection matte by tag or layer mask (API / output presets). Motion Vectors photo_motion.exr 16-bit half EXR HDRP only (Unity's AOV pass). Files are named from the beauty capture plus a layer suffix, with the same collision-safe counter naming as photos. Unity's EXR encoder writes single-part files, so layers are per-pass files by design — the naming keeps them grouped.

At runtime — Capture tab → Export Layers , then tick the layers you want. Unsupported layers on the active pipeline simply don't appear. In the Capture Studio / shot lists — every output preset has a Layers mask (plus matte tag / layer-mask fields); "Render All" writes the layer set beside every shot in the matrix, headless runs included. From script: var controller = PhotoModeController . Instance ; controller . LayerExportMask = PhotoModeRenderLayerMask . Depth | PhotoModeRenderLayerMask . Normal | PhotoModeRenderLayerMask . ObjectId ; controller . MatteTag = "Player" ; // optional Matte layer selection controller . CapturePhoto (); PhotoModeController.ActiveLayerCapabilities reports what the active pipeline can produce.

The exported set is a standard multi-pass workflow — here is the classic routine in any node compositor (Nuke, Fusion, After Effects with plugins, Blender's compositor): Relight from Normals + Depth. Feed photo_normal.exr into a relight node (or compute dot(N, L) in an expression) to add a light that was never in the scene; use photo_depth.exr to attenuate it by distance. Depth-of-field in post. Drive a lens-blur node with photo_depth.exr as the focus map — pick focus after the shot, at any aperture, without re-rendering. Pull a matte from Object IDs. Keying the exact color listed in photo_id_map.json isolates one object; grade the subject and the background separately, or cut the subject onto a new backdrop with photo_alpha.png . Rebuild the grade from Albedo. photo_albedo.png is the texture color before lighting — divide the beauty by it for a lighting-only pass, or use it as an ID-independent base for restyling.

URP / Built-in — depth, normals, albedo, object IDs, alpha and mattes all ship. The capture path executes directly on the graphics device: no renderer feature is installed and your URP renderer asset is untouched (byte-identical, asserted by test). HDRP — albedo, normals, depth and motion vectors go through Unity's own AOV pipeline; object IDs and mattes use the shared capture path. Alpha is gated (HDRP has no clean-alpha capture, matching transparent capture). Albedo and normals read the standard material properties ( _MainTex / _BaseMap , _BumpMap ); heavily custom shaders fall back to white albedo / geometric normals for those objects.

GPUs cap single textures around 16K; Photo Mode Pro renders past that by splitting the frame into a grid of frustum-offset tiles and streaming them straight into the PNG on disk — 32,768 × 32,768 and beyond on commodity hardware , with peak memory bounded by one tile row, not the image. Other capture assets are supersampling wrappers capped by what the GPU can allocate in one texture. The one true tiler on GitHub is an Editor-only Unity Recorder plugin — and it does not solve post-processing across tile seams, which is the actually hard part. Photo Mode Pro does; the rules below are the engineering.

Runtime — Capture tab → the TILED row: 8K (7680×4320), 16K (15360×8640) or 32K (30720×17280). The processing badge shows while the grid renders; wall time, tile count and measured peak memory are logged. Capture Studio / shot lists — tick Tiled on an output preset (or just set dimensions beyond the GPU limit; the studio routes automatically). Tiled outputs stream to PNG — EXR needs the whole frame in memory, so the combination is reported rather than silently degraded. Script — PhotoModeTiledCapture.Capture(camera, adjustments, backend, width, height, directory, fileName) returns the path, tile count, wall time and measured peak memory.

Screen-space post-processing is wrong at naive tile boundaries: a vignette evaluated per tile darkens every tile's edges; grain restarts its noise field at every seam; a depth-of-field kernel at a tile border blurs against nothing. Photo Mode Pro applies one rule per effect class: Full-frame-UV effects (vignette, grain) are taken out of the pipeline during tile renders and re-evaluated against full-frame coordinates in a per-tile overlay pass — the falloff and the noise field are continuous across seams by construction . The vignette uses the same falloff as the pipeline's; grain uses the package's own full-frame noise field, so its character differs marginally from the pipeline's texture-based grain. The overlay also applies the vignette after tonemapping rather than before it as the pipeline does, so with Neutral or ACES tonemapping a tiled export's vignette reads slightly flatter than the preview's. Depth of field renders with an overlap margin (64 px) that is cropped away — the blur kernel sees real context past the seam instead of blurring against nothing. Effects that cannot be made seam-correct are disabled for tiled output rather than rendered wrong: bloom, chromatic aberration, lens distortion and motion blur are turned off during the tile renders (a bloom halo or a distortion warp evaluated per tile would repeat at every seam). The presenter-pass extras — sharpen, tilt-shift, the HSL qualifier — and LUT filters are likewise not applied to tiled output . All of these still appear in normal (non-tiled) captures. A regression test renders a tiled capture with strong vignette and grain and asserts pixel continuity across every seam, and a tiled 4×4 render is asserted to match a single-pass render of the same resolution within tolerance.

Output is 8-bit RGBA PNG, written by the package's own scanline-streaming encoder (pure Unity/BCL — no third-party code) so the full image never exists in memory. Rendering pauses the game thread for the duration; a 32K capture takes on the order of a minute depending on scene and disk. Motion-dependent effects (temporal AA) are not part of tile renders.

The Gallery tab browses everything captured on this device: a thumbnail grid with paging, favorites, newest/oldest/favorites-first sorting, a fullscreen viewer, and per-photo capture metadata. Fully gamepad-navigable like every other tab. Open full-size — click a thumbnail once to select it, again to view it fullscreen; the viewer pages with prev/next, shows an index counter and the photo's filename and capture time, and closes with CLOSE or Esc. Multi-select — long-press any thumbnail for one second to enter selection mode (the held photo is ticked); click toggles further photos; Esc, CANCEL or unticking the last photo exits. Favorite / Delete — favorites sort to the front in FAVS mode; deleting removes the photo, its metadata and any exported render layers that belong to it. Every delete is two-step: the first press arms the button as an inline confirmation with a visible 3.5-second countdown, the second press executes — there is no way to lose photos to a single slip. Adaptive grid — thumbnails keep each photo's true aspect ratio in a three-column grid (rows size to their tallest cell, 12 photos per page), so portrait, square and ultrawide shots all read correctly. Go To Shot — every capture stores its camera position, rotation and lens in a sidecar; one press re-frames the live photo camera to exactly where a saved shot was taken, ready to re-shoot with a different look. Share hook — PhotoModeController.OnPhotoCaptured provides the file path for platform share integrations; the package deliberately implements no platform's share sheet itself. Photos stay ordinary PNGs in the save folder. Metadata lives in a <photo>.png.meta.json sidecar (schema-versioned JSON); thumbnails are cached in memory behind an LRU bound, so a library of thousands of photos cannot exhaust memory.

Photo mode freezes the world — the scrubber lets you move it, one frame at a time. While photo mode is open, every Animator and every Timeline (PlayableDirector) in the scene is snapshotted and halted, and the Camera tab's SCRUB controls step any of them to an exact frame: catch the apex of a jump, the crack of an impact, the exact blink you want. TARGET cycles the scrubbable things in the scene. Scrub samples the target deterministically — the same slider value always lands on the same pose, even at timeScale = 0 , forwards or backwards. Physics is frozen for the session (rigidbodies go kinematic), so ragdolls and props hold still while you work. On exit everything restores exactly: animator speeds, update modes and states, director times, rigidbody flags and velocities — the same restore contract as the camera, audio and time scale. From script: PhotoModeController.Instance.Scrubber exposes Targets and Scrub(target, normalizedTime) .

Everything in the UI is also available from script. The whole public surface lives on PhotoModeController (namespace PhotoModePro ), reached via the static PhotoModeController.Instance . Instance is assigned in the controller's OnEnable , so it can still be null in your own Awake / OnEnable ; subscribe from Start() or null-check first.

C# event Signature Fires OnEntered Action Photo mode entered. OnExited Action Photo mode exited (state already restored). OnPhotoCaptured Action<string, Texture2D> A photo was saved (path and thumbnail). The thumbnail is owned by photo mode and destroyed on the next capture or on exit (copy it to keep it), and can be null even for a saved photo. OnAdjustmentsReplaced Action The adjustment values were replaced wholesale (preset applied or reset). Three of these also exist as serialized UnityEvents on the component for Inspector-only wiring: On Entered , On Exited and On Photo Captured (a PhotoCapturedUnityEvent , i.e. UnityEvent<string, Texture2D> ). The C# event fires first, then the UnityEvent. using PhotoModePro ; using UnityEngine ; void Start () { // From Start(), Instance is already assigned (it is set in the // controller's OnEnable). var controller = PhotoModeController . Instance ; controller . OnEntered += () => Debug . Log ( "Photo mode open" ); controller . OnExited += () => Debug . Log ( "Photo mode closed" ); controller . OnPhotoCaptured += ( path , thumb ) => Debug . Log ( $"Saved {path}" ); }

t: Enter / exit from a pause menu
b: EnterPhotoMode() , ExitPhotoMode() and TogglePhotoMode() are plain public methods. Wire them to a button or call them from your game-state machine: using PhotoModePro ; public void OnPhotoModeButtonClicked () { pauseMenu . Hide (); PhotoModeController . Instance . EnterPhotoMode (); } void Start () { // Reopen the pause menu when the player leaves photo mode. // Subscribed from Start(): Instance is not assigned until the // controller's OnEnable has run. PhotoModeController . Instance . OnExited += pauseMenu . Show ; } Both methods are safe to spam: EnterPhotoMode() no-ops when already active (or when no main camera exists), ExitPhotoMode() no-ops while inactive or while a capture is in progress. IsActive and IsCapturing report the current state. See Integrations for the full pause-menu pattern.

If a photo mode binding doubles as a gameplay action (the demo's Space is both fly-up and jump), the closing key press would otherwise bleed into gameplay on the exit frame. ExitedThisFrame is true only during that single frame: void Update () { var photoMode = PhotoModeController . Instance ; if ( photoMode != null && ( photoMode . IsActive || photoMode . ExitedThisFrame )) return ; // photo mode owns input this frame // ... gameplay input ... } The demo's ThirdPersonCharacter uses exactly this pattern.

t: Audio: mixer snapshots instead of AudioListener.pause
b: By default photo mode sets AudioListener.pause on enter and restores the prior value exactly on exit. If your game drives audio through mixer snapshots, set PhotoModeSettings.AudioPauseMode to AudioPauseMode.None (the package then never touches audio) and transition in your own handlers: using PhotoModePro ; using UnityEngine.Audio ; [SerializeField] AudioMixerSnapshot pausedSnapshot ; [SerializeField] AudioMixerSnapshot gameplaySnapshot ; void Start () { var controller = PhotoModeController . Instance ; controller . OnEntered += () => pausedSnapshot . TransitionTo ( 0.1f ); controller . OnExited += () => gameplaySnapshot . TransitionTo ( 0.1f ); } More audio strategies in Integrations .

ActiveCapabilities returns the EffectCapabilities flags of the active effects backend. While photo mode is closed, it returns a cheap, side-effect-free prediction of the backend that would be selected right now: using PhotoModePro ; using PhotoModePro.Effects ; EffectCapabilities caps = PhotoModeController . Instance . ActiveCapabilities ; if (( caps & EffectCapabilities . DepthOfField ) != 0 ) { // safe to surface DoF in your own UI } bool canTransparent = ( caps & EffectCapabilities . TransparentCapture ) != 0 ; Flags: Exposure , Contrast , Saturation , Temperature , Vignette , Grain , DepthOfField , TransparentCapture , Bloom , ChromaticAberration , LensDistortion , TiltShift , Sharpen , MotionBlur , Tint , ColorBalance , Curves , HslQualifier . The matrix per pipeline is on Pipelines .

The entire photo mode UI (every panel, control, label, animation and sound) restyles from a single PhotoModeUITheme asset. Swap the asset to ship a new look.

Duplicate the shipped PhotoModeUITheme.asset (or create a fresh one via Assets > Create > Photo Mode Pro > UI Theme ). Change colors, sprites, fonts, motion and audio on the duplicate. Assign it to the Theme field on the PhotoModeUIController component of your photo mode UI prefab. The theme is applied at bind time (every time the UI spawns), so the next time photo mode opens, the whole panel wears your skin. At runtime you can also set PhotoModeUIController.Theme and call ApplyTheme() to restyle a live panel.

Colors ¶ Field Used for PanelColor Main panel background. ControlColor Slider/button/toggle backgrounds. AccentColor Fills, highlights, the selected tab. TextColor Primary labels. DimTextColor Hints and value readouts. DestructiveColor Destructive action labels and glyphs (delete, clear). DestructiveControlColor Background of destructive controls (delete, clear). Sprites and icons ¶ PanelSprite , ControlSprite and HandleSprite override the builder defaults (null keeps them). The generated 9-sliced sprites ( RoundedPanelSprite , RoundedControlSprite , GlowSprite , KnobSprite , RingSprite ) and the category icons ( CameraIcon , LightIcon , EffectsIcon , PresetsIcon , CaptureIcon , GalleryIcon , SnapIcon ) can each be replaced with your own art. Typography ¶ TmpFont sets the TextMeshPro font asset for all labels (null falls back to the TMP default). TmpOutlineMaterial is an optional TMP material with a black outline/underlay used by scene-floating text (hint chips, the toast filename) so it stays readable over bright surfaces. A legacy Font field exists as a fallback for non-TMP text. TMP Essential Resources The UI uses TextMeshPro. Import the essentials once via Window > TextMeshPro > Import TMP Essential Resources if your project has not already (the demo builder and the Setup Wizard handle this for you). Motion ¶ Field Default Meaning EnableMotion true Master switch for all UI motion. HoverScale 1.05 Control scale while hovered/selected. PressScale 0.95 Control scale while pressed. PunchAmplitude 0.08 Release punch wobble strength. TransitionDuration 0.25 s Master duration for panel/category transitions. UI audio ¶ Field Meaning EnableUiAudio Master switch for UI sounds. UiVolume 0–1 volume for all UI sounds. HoverClip / ClickClip / TabClip Hover (or gamepad selection), click/submit, category change. ToggleOnClip / ToggleOffClip Toggle switches. ShutterClip Played with the capture flash. UiMixerGroup Optional AudioMixerGroup ; null plays straight to the listener. Kill switches For a completely static, silent UI, set EnableMotion and EnableUiAudio to false. No other changes needed. Or keep motion and drop your own recorded sounds into the clip slots to replace the generated ones.

The theme restyles the photo mode panel and its floating chrome (toolbar, hint chips, toast). It does not touch your game's own UI, and gameplay HUD canvases are only ever hidden/shown by photo mode, never restyled (see Capturing photos for the visibility toggles). Related: Core Concepts · FAQ
Version 1.1 extends Photo Mode Pro beyond desktop 3D: captures work in WebGL builds, the UI is usable with touch, and orthographic (2D) games get a photo mode that behaves like one.

On WebGL there is no user-visible file system, so captures land in the persistent in-game gallery : Unity's WebGL file system is backed by IndexedDB, and Photo Mode Pro flushes it after every write and every delete , so the gallery (and your saved looks) survive page reloads. Downloading is explicit, from the gallery, when the player wants it: Download button (WebGL only) — with photos selected (or none selected for everything on the device) the gallery shows DOWNLOAD ALL / DOWNLOAD X IMAGES . Exactly one image downloads as a plain PNG; several download as one or more zip archives named PhotoModePro_Captures_<timestamp>.zip (split into _part1 , _part2 … zips for very large selections, so no single archive risks running the browser out of memory). Multi-select — long-press any thumbnail for one second to enter selection mode, then click to tick more photos; Esc, CANCEL or unticking the last photo leaves selection mode. What changes compared to desktop: The save folder row and the capture toast's reveal in file browser action are hidden — there is no file browser to open. Everything else, including render-layer EXR/PNG export and metadata sidecars, works the same (layer files stay in the gallery's storage rather than downloading individually). Super-sample and tiled resolutions are limited by the browser's GPU memory; stay at or below 2× super-sampling for a typical WebGL build. No setup is required — the platform is detected at runtime.

The UI and camera are drivable entirely by touch: One-finger drag on the viewport looks around (in 2D it pans instead). Pinch zooms (FOV in 3D, orthographic zoom in 2D). Two-finger drag pans the camera. Panel controls (sliders, toggles, tabs) respond to taps as normal pointer input; hit targets grow slightly when a touch screen is the active pointer. On narrow or portrait screens the hint-chip bar hides itself and the side panel clamps its width so the viewport stays usable. Touch input is additive: a connected gamepad or keyboard keeps working at the same time. Android is verified in-engine and in the Android emulator. iOS is expected to work through the same touch path but is not yet a supported claim — it is on the roadmap.

When photo mode opens on an orthographic camera it adapts automatically — there is nothing to configure: Pan instead of fly. Move input pans the image plane; pan speed tracks the zoom level so framing feels consistent at any magnification. Look input is ignored (a flat scene has no depth axis to swing) and roll still works for dutch angles. Zoom instead of FOV. The FOV slider relabels to Zoom and scales the camera's orthographic size proportionally — lower is tighter, matching the perspective slider's direction. Orbit and the physical camera hide. Orbiting a flat scene only shows it edge-on, and focal length/aperture have no meaning without a projection, so both are hidden for the session. Hiding 2D layers ¶ Sorting layers cannot be culled with a camera mask, so Photo Mode Pro hides them by toggling renderers. List the sorting layer names you want the Hide 2D Layers toggle to affect in your PhotoModeSettings asset under Hidden Sorting Layer Names (for example a weather overlay or foreground parallax band). Every matching renderer's prior state is restored exactly on exit; if nothing in the scene matches, the toggle hides itself. The package ships with a small 2D demo scene ( PhotoMode2DDemo ) built entirely from generated sprites.

Photo Mode Pro is built to drop into an existing game without taking it over. It requires no packages beyond Unity itself and does not edit your ProjectSettings; state is restored exactly on exit. This page covers the common integration points.

Photo Mode Pro has no hard dependency on Cinemachine (the package compiles and runs without it) but plays cleanly with it when present (the Setup Wizard detects and reports Cinemachine in its checks). What happens on enter when a CinemachineBrain drives your main camera: The main camera (carrying the brain) is disabled , which suspends Cinemachine's hold on the rendered view. The brain component itself is never touched, removed or disabled. The photo camera is a clean clone: it carries no CinemachineBrain , so virtual cameras cannot pull it around. The free camera owns its transform entirely while photo mode is open. On exit, the main camera's enabled state is restored exactly and Cinemachine resumes control as if nothing happened. Your virtual cameras keep running throughout (handy with the Unscaled pause mode, where blends continue). Note If your vcams animate on scaled time, the default TimeScaleZero pause freezes them along with the rest of the game, which is usually exactly what a photo mode should do. If you use URP camera stacking alongside (or instead of) Cinemachine, your overlay stack is untouched too; see the per-pipeline notes .

The input layer is abstracted behind version defines and works with all three Active Input Handling settings (the Setup Wizard verifies your configuration): Project setting Status Input System Package (new) Recommended. Full keyboard, mouse and gamepad support. Input Manager (legacy) Supported, with the gamepad limitation below. Both Supported; the new Input System backend is used. Legacy Input Manager gamepad limitation On the legacy Input Manager, gamepad right-stick look and triggers are unavailable : the default InputManager.asset defines no axes for them, and the package does not edit your ProjectSettings. Keyboard + mouse is fully supported; gamepad UI navigation then uses the default Horizontal/Vertical axes, which also drive camera movement. See the support matrix . Key and gamepad bindings live on the settings asset ( ToggleKey / ToggleButton , CaptureKey / CaptureButton , HideUiKey / HideUiButton ).

PhotoModeSettings.AudioPauseMode picks the strategy: Mode Behavior AudioListenerPause (default) AudioListener.pause is set on enter; the prior value is restored exactly on exit, so a game that was already paused stays paused. None Photo mode never touches audio. Drive your own transitions from the enter/exit events. The mixer-snapshot pattern with None : using PhotoModePro ; using UnityEngine.Audio ; [SerializeField] AudioMixerSnapshot pausedSnapshot ; [SerializeField] AudioMixerSnapshot gameplaySnapshot ; void Start () { var controller = PhotoModeController . Instance ; controller . OnEntered += () => pausedSnapshot . TransitionTo ( 0.1f ); controller . OnExited += () => gameplaySnapshot . TransitionTo ( 0.1f ); } UI sounds (hover, click, shutter) are separate and can be routed into a mixer group of your choice via the theme; see Theming .

Treat photo mode as one more state your game can be in, owned by your state machine: using PhotoModePro ; public class GameStateMachine : MonoBehaviour { void Start () { var photoMode = PhotoModeController . Instance ; photoMode . OnEntered += () => SetState ( GameState . PhotoMode ); photoMode . OnExited += () => SetState ( GameState . Paused ); // back to the menu } public void OnPhotoModeButtonClicked () { HidePauseMenu (); PhotoModeController . Instance . EnterPhotoMode (); } // ... } Practical notes: Already-paused games: photo mode records Time.timeScale on enter and restores that exact value on exit. Entering from a timeScale = 0 pause menu and exiting back to it is fully supported. Disable the built-in toggle if you want exclusive control: the controller polls its toggle binding whenever a settings asset is assigned. Pick a toggle key that does not collide with your menus, or gate entry entirely through your own UI and pick an unused binding. Shared bindings: if any photo mode binding doubles as a gameplay action, use the ExitedThisFrame guard; see Events & API . Hide your HUD: add your HUD canvases to the controller's Game Ui Canvases list (or tag them and set GameUiTag ) so photo mode can hide them; they are restored exactly on exit. Scene changes: replacing or unloading a scene while photo mode is open auto-closes it cleanly, so loading screens and level transitions need no special handling. Additive loads (streamed chunks) don't interrupt the session. Related: Core Concepts · Pipelines · Troubleshooting

Photo Mode Pro detects the active render pipeline at runtime and picks the right effects backend automatically. Controls for effects the active backend cannot apply hide themselves ( PhotoModeController.ActiveCapabilities exposes the same flags to scripts).

Effect URP HDRP Built-in (PPv2) Built-in (fallback) Exposure ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Contrast ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Saturation ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Temperature ✓ ✓ ✓ — Vignette ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Film grain ✓ ✓ ✓ — Depth of field ✓ ✓ ✓ — Bloom ✓ ✓ ✓ — Chromatic aberration ✓ ✓ ✓ — Lens distortion ✓ ✓ ✓ — Tint ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Color balance ✓ ✓ ✓ — RGB curves ✓ ✓ — — Motion blur ✓ ✓ — — Tilt-shift ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Sharpen ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ HSL qualifier ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Transparent capture ✓ — ✓ ✓ Tilt-shift, sharpen and the HSL qualifier render through the package's own pipeline-independent presenter pass, which is why every backend has them; LUT filters take the same path and are likewise available on all four backends.

Effects run through a code-built global Volume at very high priority. No scene assets are touched, and everything is removed on exit. URP's film grain reads weaker than PPv2's at the same intensity, so the URP backend uses a coarse grain lookup ( Large01 ) with a low luminance response to match the PPv2 look. URP's own depth-of-field aperture parameter floors at f/1.0 , so the bottom of the shared f/0.7–f/16 range renders slightly deeper focus on URP than on HDRP (where f/0.7 is the physical camera's true floor). Camera stacking is safe. The photo camera renders as a normal Base camera; your main camera's overlay stack is left untouched while photo mode is open and is intact after exit (asserted by HostileEnvironmentTests.UrpOverlayCameraStack_UnaffectedAfterExit in the release test suite).

Depth of field drives the physical camera ( Camera.aperture , focalLength ); the package keeps physical properties enabled while applying adjustments so FOV smoothing can't silently kill DoF. Exposure maps to ColorAdjustments.postExposure (relative EV, same semantics as URP) rather than HDRP's absolute scene Exposure override, so the slider behaves identically across pipelines and never fights auto-exposure. Transparent capture is unsupported. Clean alpha would require an alpha-capable color buffer format on the HDRP asset, which the package does not edit. The Transparent BG toggle hides automatically. The demo's panoramic skybox material has no effect on HDRP (HDRP uses volume skies); after a rebuild for HDRP the demo uses HDRP's default sky.

t: Built-in with Post Processing Stack v2
b: The backend creates its own PostProcessVolume , profile and PostProcessLayer on the photo camera, giving the full adjustment set except RGB curves and motion blur : PPv2's motion blur needs motion vectors a frozen scene does not produce, and its spline-based curves predate the TextureCurve model the package drives. Both controls hide automatically on PPv2. PPv2's vignette reads weaker than URP's at the same intensity, so the slider value is boosted internally toward the URP look; expect subtle character differences between pipelines at identical slider values.

An internal full-screen shader provides exposure, contrast, saturation, vignette and tint, and the pipeline-independent presenter adds tilt-shift, sharpen, the HSL qualifier and LUT filters; transparent capture also works. Temperature, film grain, depth of field, bloom, chromatic aberration, lens distortion, color balance, RGB curves and motion blur are unavailable and their controls hide automatically. Install com.unity.postprocessing for the full set; the Setup Wizard's effects-backend check links you straight to the Package Manager.

The aperture property accepts any positive value, but backends clamp it into f/0.7–f/16 when applying ( the effects how-to explains why ). Out-of-range values from old presets or scripts are clamped and never raise an error.

Demo materials are generated for the active pipeline (Standard, URP Lit or HDRP Lit). Opening the demo scene under a mismatched pipeline offers Rebuild demo for current pipeline ; the Setup Wizard's demo check offers the same rebuild. See Troubleshooting if the demo ever renders pink.
